# Getting On The Net
This guide covers the basics of using headsets and AN/PRC-117G radios.
If you are new to the communications system, start here. For detailed radio controls, see the [textlink="AN/PRC-117G Radio" link="AU14CommsANPRC"] guide.
## Check your equipment
Most roles begin with a [bold]field headset[/bold] in the ears slot.
This is your personal radio and is sufficient for normal squad communications.
CLF characters instead use a concealable earpiece attached to their clothing. It works similarly to a headset but does not occupy the ears slot. See [textlink="Field Headsets" link="AU14CommsHeadsets"] for details.
Some roles also receive an [bold]AN/PRC-117G[/bold] manpack radio.
A manpack can:
- transmit on loaded radio nets - provide relay coverage to nearby headsets - carry several radio nets at once - provide access to additional communications functions
If you only have a headset, continue to [bold]Using your headset[/bold].
If you also have an AN/PRC, continue through the manpack sections below.
## Relay coverage
Combat radio nets are [bold]relay-gated[/bold].
A headset cannot communicate across the map by itself. It must be within range of a relay carrying the same net.
Combat nets can be relayed by:
- a powered AN/PRC worn by a trained operator - a deployed retransmission station - a command-post antenna mast - a powered shipboard communications array - a vehicle radio - an engineering field antenna mast - a CLF clandestine base station - a staked CLF relay set - a mast or array carrying a CLF splice
Without a suitable relay in range, the combat net cannot transmit or receive through your headset.
Colony and civilian channels are different.
They are not relay-gated, but they are also not private.
### Relay range
Standard relay coverage is divided into clear and degraded ranges.
[bold]Distance[/bold]
[bold]Signal[/bold]
0-30 tiles
Clear traffic.
30-45 tiles
Degraded traffic. Some words may be lost.
Beyond 45 tiles
No connection.
Relay coverage normally extends one level above and below the source.
Areas separated vertically, such as tunnels or lower decks, may therefore require additional relays.
Shipboard communications arrays can cover an entire site vertically.
## Using your headset
With your headset equipped, type:
[color=#a4885c]:h Radio check, over.[/color]
The important part is:
[color=#a4885c]:h[/color]
This sends the following message over the headset's default radio net.
If the net has relay coverage, other listeners on that net receive the message under your callsign.
Headsets may contain several nets.
Examine your headset to see its available radio prefixes.
Common examples include:
- [color=#a4885c]:v[/color] - command, if the headset contains the command key - [color=#a4885c]:a[/color] - Alpha, if the headset contains the Alpha key
A headset can only access nets for which it contains the appropriate key.
Headset keys cannot normally be added in the field.
Radio messages use your [bold]callsign[/bold], not your character name.
Normal face-to-face speech is unaffected.
## Using an AN/PRC-117G
Operating the AN/PRC directly requires radio-operator training.
[bold]Faction[/bold]
[bold]Trained roles[/bold]
[bold]GOVFOR and OPFOR[/bold]
Commander, Adjutant, staff officers, engineering officers, intelligence officers, synthetics, squad leaders, Fireteam Leaders, and Radio Traffic Operators.
[bold]CLF[/bold]
Cell Leader and Radio Operator.
GOVFOR and OPFOR use the same radio training.
A trained operator can therefore operate a captured AN/PRC from either side.
Untrained characters cannot open the radio panel or transmit directly through the manpack.
They can still:
- use another operator's handset - gain radio training by reading a [bold]field radio operator's pamphlet[/bold]
### Opening the radio
To operate the manpack:
- wear the AN/PRC in your [bold]back slot[/bold] - alt-click the radio, or open its verb menu - select [bold]Open Radio Panel[/bold]
A radio in your hands, inside storage, or on the ground does not function as a worn manpack.
The first time the panel is opened, a short briefing appears.
[bold]? HELP[/bold] opens the briefing again later.
The status banner below the radio display reports problems preventing normal operation.
A green banner indicates that the radio is ready.
## Load your nets
A worn AN/PRC relays every friendly combat net loaded into its memory.
Loaded nets therefore affect both the operator and nearby headset users.
For normal setup, press:
[bold]LOAD STANDARD NETS[/bold]
This:
- switches the radio on - loads your squad net - loads your faction's command net - selects your squad net as the working memory
Existing manually configured memories are not overwritten.
The command also does not reset the radio's waveform, encryption state, or output settings.
### Loading a net manually
On the [bold]NETS[/bold] tab:
- select [bold]+ ADD MEMORY[/bold] - give the memory a short label - select [bold]EDIT[/bold] - choose a net - select [bold]USE[/bold] if you want to transmit through it
Your squad net is marked [bold][YOUR SQUAD][/bold].
The working memory is marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
Loading a net does not automatically make it the working memory.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] always transmits through the memory marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
Memories can also be renamed, emptied, or deleted.
Direct frequencies are configured through the [textlink="expert faceplate" link="AU14CommsANPRCExpert"].
## Load your COMSEC fill
Most faction radio traffic is encrypted.
The AN/PRC receives its faction encryption key from a physical [bold]COMSEC fill card[/bold].
To load a fill:
- find your issued fill card - use it on the radio - open the [bold]SECURITY[/bold] tab - confirm that the radio reads [bold]ENCRYPTED[/bold]
The radio can still transmit without a valid fill.
Traffic sent over a secured faction net without the correct fill is transmitted in the clear.
This means:
- compatible receivers can read the message - the transmission produces a direction-finding signature
Check the SECURITY tab if the radio warns about its encryption state.
## Transmitting through the manpack
Once a working memory is selected, type:
[color=#a4885c]:r HAVOC 6, this is ALPHA ROMEO, radio check, over.[/color]
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] transmits through whichever memory is marked [bold]ON AIR[/bold].
The [bold]TALK[/bold] line on the radio display also shows the active transmission net.
Select another memory with [bold]USE[/bold] before transmitting if you need to change nets.
A worn radio normally uses the [bold]wearer's callsign[/bold].
The guided panel displays this as [bold]AUTO[/bold].
If no callsign is assigned, the radio identifies the operator as [bold]UNKNOWN STATION[/bold].
## Radio check
The AN/PRC includes a built-in [bold]RADIO CHECK[/bold] function.
It transmits:
[bold]RADIO CHECK, HOW COPY, OVER[/bold]
on the current working net.
Afterward, the radio privately reports:
- which stations received the transmission - whether each station received it clearly or degraded
This includes ordinary headset and earpiece users.
RADIO CHECK can therefore confirm whether the current net has working coverage without requiring another player to answer manually.
If used inside an enemy jammer field, the report also provides an approximate bearing toward the strongest jammer.
## Handset
The handset allows someone to use an AN/PRC without radio-operator training.
It can also provide access to a net that is not available through the user's own headset.
To take the handset:
- stand within roughly two and a half tiles of the radio or its wearer - have a free hand - alt-click the wearer or deployed radio - select [bold]Take Handset[/bold]
[bold]Normal speech while holding the handset is transmitted through the radio.[/bold]
A radio prefix is not required.
Whispering remains local and does not transmit.
The handset:
- transmits through the radio's ON AIR memory - uses the holder's callsign - can only be held by one person at a time - automatically returns if the holder moves beyond the cord's range
Select [bold]Hang Up Handset[/bold] to return it manually.
If you are wearing your own AN/PRC while holding another radio's handset, your own manpack takes priority.
## CLF communications
The CLF do not have a permanent communications array.
Their combat-net coverage comes from deployable equipment or from hostile communications infrastructure that has been tapped.
A CLF cell can begin with:
- an AN/PRC manpack - a clandestine base station - a net splice kit - two relay sets
These are issued through the Cell Leader or Radio Operator, depending on which roles are present.
The issued manpack begins tuned to both the cell net and cell command.
Additional communications equipment can be constructed at a sapper's workbench or purchased through Special Equipment.
### CLF relay equipment
A [bold]field antenna mast[/bold] provides:
- 75 tiles of clear coverage - degraded coverage out to 100 tiles
A field mast:
- must be constructed outdoors - requires engineering training - requires power - only carries faction nets whose COMSEC key has been loaded into it - can be damaged, re-keyed, or tapped by either side
Cell Leaders, Radio Operators, Guerillas, and Machine Gunners can construct field masts.
See [textlink="the AN/PRC-117G guide" link="AU14CommsANPRC"] for mast construction.
A [bold]clandestine base station[/bold] provides:
- 55 tiles of clear coverage - degraded coverage out to 80 tiles - a usable handset
It is too heavy to conceal on a person.
A [bold]relay set[/bold] provides:
- 35 tiles of clear coverage - degraded coverage out to 50 tiles
Relay sets have no local controls and can be useful inside buildings, tunnels, and other areas unsuitable for field masts.
Only the Cell Leader and Radio Operator can stake down a relay set or base station.
### Keying a field mast
Field antenna masts carry only factions whose COMSEC keys are loaded into the mast.
To add the CLF key to an existing field mast:
- open the feed using a screwdriver and wirecutters - use a CLF fill card on the open feed - close the feed with a screwdriver - seal it with a welder
The mast goes off the air while its feed is open.
This requires engineering training.
Using a multitool on an open feed removes all stored keys.
Adding a CLF key does not remove any existing faction keys.
## CLF net splicing
Fixed communications masts and site arrays can be tapped with a [bold]net splice kit[/bold].
A successful splice adds CLF combat nets to the structure's existing relay coverage.
It does not remove or disrupt the nets already carried by the structure.
A command-post mast provides approximately 75 tiles of coverage.
A site array provides approximately 200 tiles.
Splicing requires:
- a net splice kit - the [bold]Radio Operator[/bold] role
Use the kit on a compatible mast or array to open the splice interface.
### Finding trunk carriers
The splice interface hides several trunk carriers across the band.
Use:
- [bold]PROBE[/bold] - check a position in the band - [bold]LOCK[/bold] - attempt to capture a carrier
Stronger probe results indicate that a carrier is closer.
A result of zero means there is no carrier within thirty positions of the selected point.
A LOCK succeeds if the selected position is within three positions of the carrier.
Failed locks:
- consume two probes - significantly increase the detection meter
Probe uses are shared across the entire attempt.
If all probes are consumed or the detection meter fills, the splice fails.
Failure:
- consumes the splice kit - places the junction into a 90-second fault state - prevents another splice attempt during that period
The junction produces visible sparks during the splice attempt and fault state.
### Protecting CLF relay equipment
CLF communications equipment is physically vulnerable.
A completed [bold]splice[/bold] remains visible on the mast.
Someone standing beside it can:
- shoot it - remove it
Removing a splice takes approximately eight seconds and returns its keying module.
Opening the feed of a spliced [bold]field antenna mast[/bold] also knocks the tap loose, and its keying module drops at the foot of the mast.
The recovered module can read CLF traffic until CLF leadership performs a recrypto.
A deployed [bold]relay set[/bold] can also be packed up by anyone.
Packing it takes approximately three seconds.
## Troubleshooting
If communications are not working, check the following common problems.
[bold]Symptom[/bold]
[bold]Check[/bold]
Nobody answers on a combat net
Move closer to a relay carrying that net.
[color=#a4885c]:r[/color] uses the wrong net
Check which memory is marked ON AIR and select the correct memory with USE.
The radio panel will not open
Check that the AN/PRC is worn in your back slot and that you have radio-operator training.
Traffic is broken or full of static
You may be near the edge of relay coverage or inside a jammer field.
AN/PRC traffic is pure static
The transmitting and receiving radios may not have matching COMSEC keys.
Your headset cannot access a net
Examine the headset and check its installed keys. Use a handset if you need temporary access to another net.
You transmit as UNKNOWN STATION
You do not currently have an assigned callsign.
Local speech is being transmitted
Check whether you are holding a radio handset. Hang it up or whisper for local speech.
The AN/PRC stops operating
Check its power cell. Searching and high output power increase battery consumption.
